t: Day 8 - An In-depth Analysis of The Bread and The Wine | Module 8
s: A line-by-line spiritual breakdown of the communion elements under the Order of Melchizedek, detailing seven distinct spiritual properties within the heavenly bread and six within the heavenly wine to transform communion from an empty ritual into a tool for deliverance, wealth creation, and spiritual authority.
r: Isaiah 51:2 · Genesis 14:17-20 · Matthew 13:33 · John 6:33 · Matthew 26:26 · Matthew 15:22-27 · Exodus 25:30 · Exodus 33 · Matthew 4:4 · Deuteronomy 8:18 · Ephesians 5:18-20 · Matthew 12:28 · John 14 · Matthew 26:27 · Luke 4:18 · Ecclesiastes 9:7 · Nehemiah 8:10 · 1 Kings 21
pts: The speaker argues that the church cannot have Jesus as a Melchizedek head while the church functions as a Levitical body, meaning leaders and believers must transition from the Old Covenant Levitical mindset into the Melchizedek priesthood.

Genesis 14 records that Melchizedek met Abraham with bread and wine before the King of Sodom arrived with worldly riches, and consuming this heavenly meal gave Abraham the spiritual fortitude to reject Sodom's corrupt wealth.

The Hebrew root for bread (lechem) connects to battling, prevailing, and overcoming (lacham), signifying that the bread represents supernatural strength to conquer enemies and break demonic oppression.
The Hebrew root for wine (yayin) refers to effervescence and bubbling, signifying supernatural increase, multiplication, and the continuous expansion of God's life.

The seven dimensions of the Heavenly Bread are: (1) the doctrine and governance of the Kingdom of God, (2) the literal Bread of Life received by faith, (3) deliverance from demonic oppression as the 'children's bread', (4) the perpetual manifest presence of God (the showbread), (5) the living Word of God, (6) spiritual prosperity through the daily rhema word, and (7) material prosperity and the divine ability to create wealth.

The speaker insists that Jesus did not say the bread is a mere symbol or representation of His body, but declared 'This is my body,' requiring believers to partake with deep reverence rather than casual church ritualism.

The six dimensions of the Heavenly Wine are: (1) the Spirit of the Kingdom (the Holy Spirit as the power and guarantor of inheritance), (2) spiritual intoxication (altering spiritual perception to see people and situations through God's perspective), (3) the blood of the covenant, (4) the anointing of the Holy Spirit to perform greater works, (5) the joy of the Lord grounded in the knowledge that God has accepted your work, and (6) generational blessings that secure ancestral inheritance like Naboth's vineyard.

The speaker argues that when Abraham partook of Melchizedek's bread and wine in Genesis 14, he spiritually consumed the body and blood of Christ and became born again prior to the establishment of the Mosaic law.
The Holy Spirit is identified as the most unrecognized person in church ministry; without active, relational communion (koinonia) and daily conversation with Him, the church operates without power.
Communion functions as a practical weapon of deliverance that shifts spiritual atmospheres and expels demonic oppression from homes and hotel rooms.

He never said, "This is a symbol of my body. This is a representation of the body." He said, "This is my body."

Faced with famine, Abraham went down to Egypt out of panic rather than relying on God's kingdom provision.

The wealth Abraham gained in Egypt was tainted wealth, carrying 'snakes in the money bag' such as strife and Hagar (who bore Ishmael).

t: Day 5 - The Tabernacle of David | Module 5
s: An understanding of the Tabernacle of David as a militant, 24/7 worship model powered by the Melchizedek priesthood that combines kingly governance and priestly intercession to defeat spiritual enemies.
r: Acts 15:16 · Amos 9:11-12 · 1 Chronicles 15:1 · Hebrews 10 · Psalm 40 · Psalm 110:1-4 · Revelation 22:16 · Revelation 5:5-10 · 2 Samuel 6:3-9 · Numbers 20:12 · Isaiah 9:6-7 · Psalm 22:3 · 1 Chronicles 25:1 · Isaiah 30:32 · Psalm 149:1-9
pts: Francis Myles introduces Module 5 of his curriculum on the Order of Melchizedek, presenting the Tabernacle of David as the restoration of the highest biblical order of worship.

The guest lecturer defines the Tabernacle of David not merely as an external structure, but as a continuous love affair and prophetic sound that began inside David's heart before becoming a public tent in Israel.

Citing Acts 15:16 and Amos 9:11-12, the speaker explains that God is rebuilding the fallen Tabernacle of David to re-establish spiritual authority and aggressively draw lost nations back to Himself in the kingdom era.

The speaker contrasts David's open tent—which placed the Ark of the Covenant directly in public view—with Moses' tabernacle of veils, arguing David received a prophetic download granting him permission to operate in a New Covenant dimension.

David understood through throne-room revelation (Psalm 110 and Psalm 40/Hebrews 10) that God was not pleased with animal sacrifices, but rather with the eternal priesthood of Jesus Christ according to the Order of Melchizedek.
The Tabernacle of David was designed as a militant place of spiritual war where God's scepter is extended from Zion to make His enemies a footstool.

Believers are called to operate in two dimensions: first entering the throne room as priests (seeking atonement, communion, and divine strategy) and then executing rulership as kings (issuing decrees, taking territory, and recovering losses).

Uzzah died when transporting the Ark because God must be treated as holy, God will not violate His command that the Ark be carried on priestly shoulders rather than an ox cart, and kingdom revival requires personal sacrifice rather than shortcuts.

The speaker teaches that God being 'enthroned' on praise (Psalm 22:3) stems from the Hebrew word yashab (to sit and judge), meaning high praise activates Christ's kingly authority to execute written judgments against spiritual enemies.

David had army commanders select prophetic musicians (1 Chronicles 25:1) and appointed 38,000 Levites—including 4,000 instrumentalists and 288 singers—to maintain unceasing 24/7 worship on earth modeled after the throne room.

The speaker concludes that New Testament believers are the living Ark carrying God's presence, called to shift territorial atmospheres and enforce kingdom victory through intentional prophetic worship.

Things don't end wrong, they begin wrong.
Your praise punishes the enemy.

t: Day 3 - Understanding the Kingdom | Module 3
s: A reinterpretation of the Book of Daniel as a practical blueprint of kingdom power over worldly systems, showing how the Melchizedek order serves as the operational wineskin to balance priestly prayer with kingly authority.
r: Daniel 2:31-35 · Daniel 1 · Daniel 2 · Daniel 3 · Daniel 4 · Daniel 5 · Daniel 2:46 · Revelation 6
pts: Myles argues that the Book of Daniel is not primarily a fatalistic or apocalyptic text about doomsday, but the Old Testament's foremost demonstration of the gospel of the kingdom.

He teaches that Daniel and the Hebrew boys were not victims of circumstance in Babylon, but were strategically placed by God into a 'culture of contrast' to demonstrate the superiority of God's kingdom over demonic structures.

In Daniel chapter 1, the clash of kingdoms centers on diet, which Myles identifies as a fundamental kingdom issue originating in Eden; ten days on a kingdom diet yielded ten times more wisdom and scientific acumen than the delicacies of Babylon.

In Daniel chapter 2, the clash is over the 'gates of revelation,' where God erased Nebuchadnezzar's dream from the king's memory to prove the inadequacy of Chaldean occult knowledge and set the stage for Daniel.
In Daniel chapter 3, the conflict concerns worship, showing that believers grounded in the gospel of the kingdom can withstand systemic pressure to bow to worldly authority.
In Daniel chapters 4 and 5, the battle moves to the domain of law, establishing that God's law sits supreme over human or demonic laws.

The statue in Nebuchadnezzar's dream represents decaying earthly empires, while the rock cut without human hands represents Jesus Christ, whose virgin birth initiated an ever-expanding kingdom during the era of the Roman Caesars.

When Daniel interpreted the dream, Nebuchadnezzar and his court fell on their faces, illustrating that governmental and military powers must ultimately submit to those who carry the authority of the gospel of the kingdom.

Myles explains that the gospel of the kingdom and the Order of Melchizedek are two sides of the same coin: the kingdom is the message/liquid, while the Melchizedek order is the wineskin/bottle that contains and applies it.

The Melchizedek wineskin trains believers to function seamlessly as both kings and priests, turning spiritual individuals into effective marketplace leaders and turning secular achievers into devoted worshippers.

t: The Priesthood Demands Holiness
s: Every believer is called to the royal priesthood of Melchizedek, which requires embracing biblical holiness as being strictly set apart for God's divine order rather than conforming to human methods.
r: 1 Peter 2:4 · 1 Peter 2:5 · 1 Peter 2:9 · Hebrews 7 · Malachi 3
pts: God originally intended the entire nation of Israel to be a kingdom of priests, but after their persistent attachment to Egypt, He narrowed the priestly role to the firstborn of every household.

Following the golden calf apostasy and the people's fear of God's presence, only the tribe of Levi stood on the Lord's side, resulting in God restricting the Old Covenant priesthood exclusively to the Levites.
